course_name_original: IMPATTO SULLA SOCIETA' E PROSPETTIVA STORICA DELL'INGEGNERIA ELETTRONICA (B032761)
course_name_en: IMPACT ON SOCIETY AND HISTORICAL PERSPECTIVE OF ELECTRONICS ENGINEERING (B032761)

learning_outcomes.text: Knowledge and understanding of the evolutionary processes of technology.
Knowledge and understanding of the factors that determined the success of a particular technology.
Knowledge and understanding of the contexts that initiated the 5 industrial revolutions.
Knowledge and understanding of the socio-economic implications of technological evolutions.
Ability to apply the evolutionary paradigm to various examples of technologies.
Ability to apply the social and economic context to technological innovations.
Ability to critically analyze and discuss strengths, weaknesses, and probability of success of a particular technology in its historical context.
Ability to effectively present one's ideas in an open teacher-student discussion, through tools such as workshops and report writing.
Ability to independently find information and texts on the topics covered.

syllabus_topics: The role of information engineering in the five industrial revolutions.
James Watt and the steam engine.
Thomas Alva Edison and the light bulb.
Nikola Tesla and the alternator.
Shockley, Bardeen, and Brattain and the transistor.
Alan Turing and automatic machines.
Federico Faggin and the microprocessor.
Steve Jobs and the computer.
Bill Gates and artificial intelligence.
Gro Harlem Brundtland and sustainability.
Factors that determined the success or failure of technologies.
What we can do to improve our impact on the planet.
From origins to the first industrial revolution: steam.
The evolution of science and technology from Homo Habilis to Galileo Galilei.
18th century England and the agricultural revolution.
The needs of a growing society and the first industrial revolution.
Thomas Newcomen, James Watt and the invention of the steam engine.
The entry of banks and capital into technological development.
The second industrial revolution: electricity.
Luigi Galvani, Alessandro Volta and the invention of the battery.
Thomas Alva Edison and the invention of the light bulb.
Nikola Tesla and the invention of the alternator.
The 'currents' war: AC vs DC.
Henry Ford and the assembly line.
Shockley, Bardeen, and Brattain and the transistor: the birth of electronics.
The third industrial revolution: the microprocessor and automation.
Machines intervene in repetitive and strenuous work. Globalization begins.
The importance of standards and standardization bodies: CEI, UNI, CENELEC, CEN, IEC, ISO.
Alan Turing and automatic machines.
The first computers and PLCs.
Steve Jobs and the personal computer.
Bill Gates and software engineering.
The fourth industrial revolution: interconnection and integration of processes.
Advances in artificial intelligence (AI), robotics, the Internet of Things (IoT), 3D printing, genetic engineering, quantum computers and other technologies.
Human beings return to the center of processes.
New professions and skills.
The fifth industrial revolution: sustainability.
Limited resources and happy degrowth.
From Greta Thunberg to ecological transition.
The limits of sustainability.
The fifth industrial revolution: energy transition and environmental sustainability.
Humanity's impact on climate change.
The paradigm shift, from fossil fuels to renewable sources.
New technologies for sustainability.
Enertronics, information engineering at the service of energy.
Technosauri and smartphones, or how technology evolves.
Why some technologies succeed and others, apparently equally valid, do not?
Technologies that have completed their parabola have become obsolete and replaced by others.
Technologies that have completed their parabola, have become obsolete, but survive not replaced by others.
Technologies that never started their parabola due to technological problems.
Technologies that started their parabola, but stopped it for external (non-technological) reasons.
Technologies that have completed their parabola, are obsolete, are dismissed, but are not replaced by others.
Darwinian evolution as a paradigm for understanding the evolution of technology.
And the future?
assessment_rules: Assessment is based on active participation in lessons, quizzes, discussions, group work, and presentations. A negative evaluation (Insufficient) results from serious conceptual errors or fragmented understanding. Sufficient to more than sufficient (18–22) shows elementary knowledge with some errors. Fair (23–25) means satisfactory understanding and ability to apply knowledge. Good to very good (26–28) demonstrates solid theoretical understanding and critical analysis. Excellent to outstanding (29–30 cum laude) requires complete, in-depth knowledge, flexibility, critical abilities, originality, and rigor. Cum Laude is awarded for brilliant and original work.
